posts.title: The app said your sandwich was 1,200 calories
slides: The app said your sandwich was 1,200 calories. That's the moment most people quit tracking.
Not because the number was high. Because it felt wrong, and now nothing in the log feels trustworthy.
One bad entry doesn't break the data. It breaks your confidence in the data. Those are different problems.
A wrong guess is a guess. It's supposed to be editable, not memorized.
The fix isn't a better database. It's treating every number as a draft you correct, not a fact you accept.
The people who stick with tracking aren't the ones with perfect logs. They're the ones who keep correcting theirs.
Estimates you can edit beat guesses you can't check.

posts.title: I thought home meals and restaurant meals were about the same
slides: I thought I ate about the same whether I cooked or ordered out. Then I tracked a month.
Home meals were close to what I expected. Restaurant meals were not.
Research on this is consistent: people underestimate restaurant meals by around 20% on average.
It's not one dish. Oil in the pan, sauce on the side, bread before the meal even starts. None of it looks like 'extra.'
92% of restaurant meals studied came in over a typical per-meal calorie target. Not fast food only, restaurants generally.
None of this means don't eat out. It means the guess and the plate are further apart than they feel.
A photo closes that gap faster than a mental estimate ever will.

posts.title: High protein hurts your kidneys: mostly false
slides: 'High protein hurts your kidneys.' For someone with healthy kidneys, that's mostly false.
Verdict: mostly false, for people without existing kidney disease.
The worry started from studies on people who already had impaired kidney function, not healthy lifters.

The real ceiling for most lifters isn't kidney safety. It's whether you can actually eat that much food.
If you have an existing kidney condition, this is between you and your doctor, not a slide.
What actually matters: consistent protein, spread through the day, hit through real food.

posts.title: This fruit smoothie has more sugar than 3 glazed donuts

Whole fruit and juice aren't the same. Juice removes the fiber that usually slows sugar down.
Not a reason to fear smoothies. A reason to know the number instead of assuming 'fruit' means low sugar.

posts.title: I stopped quitting my food tracker
slides: I stopped quitting my food tracker. One change did most of the work.
Every other time, I quit the same way: missed a day, felt behind, deleted the app.
The change wasn't more willpower. It was lowering the bar for what counted as 'still tracking.'
A blurry photo of a gas station sandwich still counts. A rough guess still counts.
The goal stopped being a perfect log. It became: don't go two days with nothing logged.
That one rule survived a family trip, a bad week, and a birthday, when 'perfect' never had.
Consistency beats precision, especially when precision is the reason you quit last time.

Know your number, then just get close most days.
